scenario_provenance.archetype_label: Multi-focus on Practices 3 & 4 (analyze data; interpret results)
validity_rules: OBSERVATIONAL comparison only (no random assignment -> no causal claim)
means differ but spreads overlap so an over-strong claim is refutable

sources.note: the item stem's verb must match the scored demand

prompt: In a survey of study habits, students who study mostly at night had a mean self-reported focus rating of 49 points (SD about 10) and students who study mostly in the morning had a mean of 45 points (SD about 10). A student claims: "students who study mostly at night always have a higher self-reported focus rating than students who study mostly in the morning." Which statement best justifies whether the data support this claim?

options.text: These results prove that students who study mostly at night will always outperform students who study mostly in the morning on self-reported focus rating in any future study or population.

misconception_source.label: Over-generalized beyond the data using definitive language

sources.note: 2025 CR Report: conclusions must use non-definitive language ('convincing evidence'), never 'proves'/'always'; and must not generalize beyond the studied population

options.text: On average students who study mostly at night had a higher self-reported focus rating (mean 49 vs 45), so the data support a typical difference; but because both SDs are about 10, the distributions overlap substantially, so the data do not support a claim that students who study mostly at night are always higher.

Since the mean for students who study mostly at night (49) is greater than for students who study mostly in the morning (45), every member of students who study mostly at night must have a higher self-reported focus rating than every member of students who study mostly in the morning.

misconception_source.label: Treated a difference in means as a claim about every individual value

sources.note: on-average differences must not be over-read as claims about all individual values; overlap matters

options.text: The claim is correct because students who study mostly at night clearly did better on self-reported focus rating.

misconception_source.label: Restated the claim without citing statistical evidence

sources.ref: AP_STATISTICS_2027_CED_FACT_PACK.md S4/S6 (skill 4.B; task verbs) + S10 'General exam-wide conventions'
sources.note: a justification must reference the statistical evidence, not merely restate the claim

parts.prompt: In a survey of study habits, students who study mostly at night had a mean self-reported focus rating of 49 points (SD about 10) and students who study mostly in the morning had a mean of 45 points (SD about 10). A student claims: "students who study mostly at night always have a higher self-reported focus rating than students who study mostly in the morning." Which statement best justifies whether the data support this claim?

criteria.description: Selects the justification that affirms the on-average difference while rejecting the over-strong 'always' claim due to overlap.
